passages.title: Guiding lights: a short history of the lighthouse
paras: For as long as people have travelled by sea, they have needed ways of finding their way safely back to land. The earliest aids to navigation were simply fires lit on hilltops near harbours. These had obvious weaknesses: they could only be seen on clear nights, they needed constant attention, and in bad weather, when they were most needed, they were often impossible to keep burning.

The most famous lighthouse of the ancient world stood at the entrance to the harbour of Alexandria, in Egypt. Completed in the third century BCE, it is thought to have been well over 100 metres tall, making it one of the tallest structures built by humans for many centuries. A fire burned at the top, and according to some accounts, a large mirror reflected its light out to sea. The building survived for more than a thousand years before it was gradually destroyed by a series of earthquakes.

After the fall of the Roman Empire, few new lighthouses were built in Europe for several centuries. It was only with the growth of trade in the later Middle Ages that interest revived, and towers began to appear along the busiest shipping routes. Most were built and run by private individuals or religious communities, who often charged passing ships a fee. As a result, lights were sometimes poorly maintained, and the quality of the service varied enormously from one place to another.

A major problem for lighthouse builders was the location of the most dangerous rocks, which were often far out at sea. Building a tower on a rock that was covered by the tide for much of the day was extremely difficult. The first lighthouse on one notorious reef off the south coast of England, completed in 1698, was made of wood and was swept away in a great storm just five years later, together with its builder. Later engineers learned to use interlocking blocks of granite, which were cut on land and fitted together like a puzzle, producing towers strong enough to withstand the waves.

The light itself also improved dramatically. Coal fires gave way to candles and later to oil lamps, but the real breakthrough came in the 1820s, when the French physicist Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens. Instead of a single thick piece of glass, which would have been extremely heavy, his lens was made up of a series of rings arranged around a central bulb. It captured far more of the light and concentrated it into a powerful beam that could be seen more than 30 kilometres away. Fresnel lenses were soon adopted around the world.

To allow sailors to tell one lighthouse from another, each was given its own pattern of light. Some showed a steady beam, others flashed at regular intervals, and some used colours. A sailor who saw two short flashes every ten seconds, for instance, could check a list and identify exactly which part of the coast he was approaching. This system, known as the light’s characteristic, is still in use today.

For most of their history, lighthouses depended on keepers, who lived at or near the tower and kept the light burning through the night. The work was lonely and often dangerous, particularly on offshore rocks, where keepers might be cut off by storms for weeks. During the twentieth century, however, electric lights and automatic systems gradually made keepers unnecessary. Today almost all lighthouses are automated, and satellite navigation means that ships rely on them far less than in the past. Many towers have been turned into museums or holiday accommodation, but most still shine every night, as a back-up in case modern systems fail.

passages.title: Rebuilding the reef
paras: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. They protect coastlines from waves, support fishing communities and attract millions of tourists. They are also in serious trouble. Rising sea temperatures cause corals to expel the tiny algae that live inside their tissues and provide most of their food, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures fall quickly, the corals can recover; if not, they starve and die. In recent decades, bleaching events that were once rare have become frequent, and in many regions large areas of reef have been lost.

Faced with this decline, scientists and conservation groups have developed a range of techniques to help reefs recover. The most widespread is coral gardening, which borrows its methods from agriculture. Small fragments of living coral are collected, either from healthy reefs or from pieces broken off by storms, and grown in underwater nurseries. These nurseries often look like rows of trees made of plastic pipes, with fragments hanging from the branches like decorations. After several months, when the fragments have grown large enough, divers attach them to damaged areas of reef.

Coral gardening has had notable successes, but it has one major drawback: it is slow and labour-intensive. Each fragment must be handled individually by a diver, and even a large project can only replant a few hectares a year. Since the world has lost reef on the scale of thousands of square kilometres, critics argue that gardening cannot hope to make a real difference, however well it is done. Supporters reply that it can still save particular reefs of special value, such as those that protect a village or support a local tourism industry.

To work on a larger scale, some researchers have turned to coral reproduction. Many corals reproduce by releasing enormous numbers of eggs and sperm into the water on just one or two nights each year, an event that is closely linked to the cycle of the moon. Teams now collect this spawn, raise the larvae in tanks or floating pools, and release them onto damaged reefs when they are ready to settle. Because a single spawning can produce millions of larvae, this approach could in theory restore much larger areas than gardening. The difficulty is that the vast majority of young corals die within their first year.

Other projects focus on the physical structure of the reef. When corals die, the reef’s rocky skeleton gradually breaks into loose rubble, which shifts with the waves and makes it almost impossible for young corals to attach themselves. In one Indonesian project, workers have laid thousands of small steel frames, coated with sand, over rubble fields. The frames hold the rubble in place and provide a stable surface on which coral fragments can grow. Within a few years, some of these sites have become hard to tell apart from natural reef.

Perhaps the most ambitious approach is the attempt to breed corals that can tolerate higher temperatures. Researchers have found that some corals survive bleaching events that kill their neighbours. By cross-breeding these survivors, or by exposing corals to gradually rising temperatures in the laboratory, they hope to produce populations better suited to the warmer oceans of the future. Some scientists are uneasy about this work, however, warning that it may distract attention from the real cause of the problem.

That cause is climate change, and on this point there is little disagreement. Restoration, its advocates admit, can buy time, but it cannot save reefs on its own. If ocean temperatures continue to rise, even the hardiest corals will eventually be overwhelmed. The best hope for reefs, most experts agree, lies in combining local restoration with rapid global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

passages.title: The myth of multitasking
paras: Many of us are proud of our ability to do several things at once. We answer emails during meetings, listen to podcasts while studying and check messages while talking to friends. Job advertisements regularly ask for candidates who can multitask, as if it were a skill like typing or speaking a foreign language. Yet a substantial body of research suggests that, for most people and most tasks, multitasking is something of an illusion, and an expensive one.

The central problem is that the human brain has a very limited capacity for conscious attention. When we believe we are doing two things simultaneously, we are usually switching rapidly between them. Each switch carries a cost. The brain has to stop one set of rules, retrieve another and reorient itself, and this takes time, typically a fraction of a second. A fraction of a second sounds trivial, but when switches happen hundreds of times a day, the losses add up. In one laboratory study, participants who alternated between two simple sorting tasks took around 40 per cent longer to finish than those who completed one task and then the other.

Switching also seems to make us more prone to error. When we return to a task after an interruption, we often have to work out where we were, and it is easy to skip a step or repeat one. This matters little when we are folding laundry, but a great deal when we are driving, performing surgery or flying an aircraft. It is no coincidence that industries where mistakes are dangerous tend to have strict rules limiting interruptions.

There are, however, important exceptions. Tasks that have become automatic through long practice, such as walking or, for an experienced driver, changing gear, require very little conscious attention and can be combined with other activities with little cost. The difficulty arises when two tasks compete for the same mental resources, as when we try to read a report while listening to someone speak. Both tasks involve processing language, and performance on both declines.

A further complication is that people are poor judges of their own multitasking ability. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Dr Ruth Calder found that the volunteers who rated themselves as the best multitaskers actually performed worst when they were tested. Heavy multitaskers, she discovered, were more easily distracted by irrelevant information, perhaps because constantly dividing their attention had weakened their ability to filter it. Calder is careful to point out that her results show an association, not proof that multitasking causes the problem. It may be that people who are easily distracted are drawn to multitasking in the first place.

Some researchers have identified a small group of people who seem genuinely able to perform two demanding tasks at once without loss. Dr Calder’s colleague, Martin Hesse, estimates that these “supertaskers” make up perhaps two per cent of the population. Studying them may eventually reveal how attention works, but Hesse warns that the existence of such people should not encourage the rest of us. Statistically, he points out, someone who believes they are a supertasker is almost certainly mistaken.

If multitasking is so inefficient, why is it so common? One explanation is that it feels productive. Switching between tasks provides a constant stream of small rewards, such as a new message or a completed item on a list, which can be satisfying even when overall progress is slow. Another is that modern working environments make it almost unavoidable, with notifications arriving constantly from several directions. In this sense, multitasking is often less a choice than a response to circumstances.

The practical advice that follows from this research is simple, if not always easy to follow. Where possible, we should group similar tasks together, turn off notifications during periods of concentrated work, and accept that doing one thing at a time is often the fastest way to get several things done. Employers, too, might reconsider whether the ability to multitask is really what they want from their staff, or whether the capacity to concentrate deeply would be more valuable.
